opus-5.5.text:
The way I think about it is that there are really two different optimization processes going on when you end up with a functioning adult human brain. One is what happens within a single lifetime: you're born, you take in an enormous amount of sensory data, you interact with the world, and your brain learns from that. That's the analog of training a model. But that learning doesn't start from nothing. It runs on a particular architecture, with particular learning rules, a particular arrangement of brain regions, certain inductive biases and reward signals, and the whole developmental program that wires things up before and after birth. None of that is learned within your lifetime. It was found by evolution.

So evolution isn't really doing the training. The genome is far too small to specify the brain's synaptic weights directly. You have something like a gigabyte of genetic information, much of it not even about the brain, while the adult brain has on the order of a hundred trillion synapses. What the genome encodes is closer to a recipe: the architecture, the hyperparameters, the learning algorithm, the initialization scheme. That's exactly what we mean by architecture search or neural architecture search in machine learning. You run an outer loop that tries different model designs, and for each candidate you run an inner loop that trains it and sees how well it does. Evolution is that outer loop, with natural selection as a very noisy fitness signal, and each organism's lifetime is an inner training run.

This framing matters a lot for thinking about AI timelines and compute requirements. When people compare the brain to AI systems, they often only count lifetime learning, roughly the compute the brain uses from birth to adulthood, and conclude we should already have enough compute for human-level AI. But that ignores the enormous amount of search evolution did to find a good architecture and learning algorithm in the first place. If you count that, the effective compute behind the human brain is vastly larger. The real question then becomes how much of that evolutionary search we have to redo, and how much we can shortcut with human insight, gradient-based methods, and the fact that we're not limited to the clumsy mechanism of mutation and selection.

My view is that we're not starting from scratch the way evolution did. We can be much more directed. But it's also wrong to assume the brain's efficiency is free, as if it came from a short training run alone. A lot of what makes human learning so sample-efficient is likely baked in by that outer loop, and part of the challenge in AI is recovering those advantages, whether through better architectures or by compensating with much more data and compute in the inner loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes evolution as an outer search guided by natural selection, but does not connect brain algorithms for enduringly valuable tasks to prolonged selection pressure.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes evolution’s outer-loop search for architecture and learning rules from lifetime learning as the inner training run, and says evolution is not training inherited weights.

r004.rationale: It mentions an arrangement of brain regions, but does not say specialized regions probably use different kinds of algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that when people talk about the human brain as evidence for how much compute you need to get general intelligence, they usually focus on the lifetime learning side. You know, a human gets born, they experience the world for twenty or thirty years, and by the end of that they're a pretty capable agent. And people try to estimate how many operations the brain does over that period and say, okay, that's roughly the compute required to train a general intelligence.

But I think that's missing a big part of the picture, which is that the brain you're born with is not a blank slate. Evolution has been doing an enormous amount of optimization over hundreds of millions of years, and what it has been optimizing is essentially the architecture. The learning algorithm, the connectivity patterns, the inductive biases, the reward signals, what you pay attention to, how your visual cortex is wired up before you've ever seen anything. All of that is the output of a search process that ran over an astronomical number of organisms, each one being sort of a sample in that search.

And that's very analogous to what we do in machine learning when we do architecture search or hyperparameter search. We don't just train one model. We try lots of variants, we see which ones learn more efficiently, and we keep the ones that work. Evolution is doing exactly that, except the inner loop is an organism's lifetime and the outer loop is natural selection over generations. The lifetime learning is the inner optimization, and evolution is the outer optimization that found an inner optimizer that works really well.

So the reason this matters is that if you want to estimate how much compute it takes to arrive at human-level intelligence from scratch, you can't just count the lifetime compute. You also have to account for the compute that went into finding the architecture in the first place. And if you try to estimate that, the number is enormous. You're looking at something like all the neural computation that has happened across all animals with nervous systems over evolutionary history, which is many, many orders of magnitude larger than a single human lifetime.

Now, the optimistic reading is that we don't have to replicate that search, because we're much smarter and more directed than evolution. Evolution is a very dumb optimizer. It can't look ahead, it has to work through reproduction, it gets confused by all sorts of things that have nothing to do with intelligence. Human researchers can run experiments, reason about what's going wrong, and transfer ideas across domains. So we should be able to do architecture search far more efficiently. But it does mean that the gap between "brain-scale compute" and "human-level AI" is not nearly as small as the naive lifetime estimate would suggest. There's a large unknown term there, which is how much of evolution's work we've already recovered with things like transformers and gradient descent, and how much is still left to find.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is that evolution is searching over the machinery that makes learning possible, rather than directly searching over everything that an individual knows. Your genes don’t specify all the connections in your adult brain. They specify a developmental process, a broad architecture, and learning rules that let the brain adapt to its environment.

That’s similar to what we do in machine learning when we search over architectures or training algorithms. There’s an outer loop where we choose how a system should learn, and an inner loop where that system actually learns from data. In the evolutionary case, natural selection is the outer loop, and learning during an organism’s lifetime is the inner loop.

Of course, evolution also builds in predispositions and some behaviors, so the distinction isn’t perfectly clean. But the important point is that evolution’s enormous computational expenditure isn’t all being spent on the equivalent of training one model. A lot of it is going into discovering a system that can learn efficiently in the first place.

r003.rationale: It contrasts evolution searching over learning machinery and architecture with learning during an organism’s lifetime, rather than treating evolution as a training run whose learned parameters are inherited.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the distinction I’m trying to draw is between finding a good learning algorithm and actually running that algorithm to learn things. Evolution doesn’t directly specify all the knowledge you acquire over your lifetime. It specifies a developmental process that produces a brain with a certain architecture, learning rules, and inductive biases. Then, as you interact with the world, that brain learns.

So you can think of evolution as an outer optimization loop, searching over systems that can learn effectively. Your individual learning is the inner loop. That’s analogous to architecture search in machine learning, where you try different architectures or training procedures, train the resulting systems, and use their performance to decide which designs to keep.

The analogy isn’t exact, because evolution also builds in some behaviors and predispositions. But it matters when we talk about how much computation was needed to produce human intelligence. The computation spent discovering a good learning system is different from the computation needed to train one once you have its design. We shouldn’t automatically assume that reproducing human abilities requires repeating the entire evolutionary search.

r001.rationale: It describes evolution as searching for effective learning systems, but does not attribute sophisticated brain algorithms to prolonged selection pressure on enduringly valuable tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the genome’s information capacity or its inability to encode many trained brain parameters.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes evolution’s outer search for a brain architecture and learning rules from individual learning as the inner loop, and says evolution does not directly specify lifetime-acquired knowledge.

r004.rationale: It mentions brain architecture and learning rules generally, but does not infer that specialized brain regions probably use different algorithms.
